references.text: Isaiah uses the same expression about making one's face hard as flint, which reflects Jesus' determined attitude when he set his face toward Jerusalem. The Greek ἐστήρισεν τὸ πρόσωπον (to set one's face) is an echo of Isaiah's prophecy concerning the Lord's servant.
Jacob turned his face toward the mountain (set his face), a parallel to the Hebrew expression for making a firm decision in a certain direction, just as Jesus set his face toward Jerusalem.
Ezekiel is told to turn his face toward Jerusalem, a prophetic expression corresponding to Jesus' decision to go to Jerusalem.
The context explains that the people of a Samaritan village did not welcome Jesus because his face was set toward Jerusalem (τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ ἦν πορευόμενον εἰς Ἰερουσαλήμ).
Jesus continued his journey toward Jerusalem, teaching through towns and villages along the way – part of the great travel narrative that begins in 9:51.
Luke again reminds us that Jesus was on his way to Jerusalem, as part of the structural travel motif that starts in 9:51.
Jesus explains to his disciples what awaits him in Jerusalem – suffering, death, and resurrection – which is precisely the content of the 'assumption' (ἀνάλημψις) mentioned in 9:51.
Jesus goes up to Jerusalem, which is the climax of the journey that began in 9:51.
Jesus' ascension (taking up) fulfills the ἀνάλημψις from 9:51. The day of his taking up was completed when he was taken into heaven.
The Acts of the Apostles refers to Jesus' ascension (ἀνελήμφθη), which is the final fulfillment of what Luke calls τῆς ἀναλήμψεως in Luke 9:51.
The very event of Jesus being taken up into heaven is described here, and it is the endpoint toward which the ἀνάλημψις in Luke 9:51 points.
Mark describes Jesus going ahead of his disciples on the road up to Jerusalem, and they were amazed – a parallel to Jesus' determined journey toward Jerusalem in Luke 9:51.
Elijah's taking up into heaven (using related Hebrew terminology) serves as a background for Luke's use of ἀνάλημψις regarding Jesus' impending ascension.
